Quillworms (Hyalinoecia) and the Australian beachworms
(Australonuphis) are among the better known Onuphidae; the
former with highly characteristic tubes (Pl. 6f) and the lat-
ter for their size (up to several metres) and occurrence on
sandy beaches and their importance as bait in fisheries. Overall,
Onuphidae vary in size from a few millimetres to several metres,
although sizes around a few centimetres are common. The ante-
riormost part is often cylindrical and widest, becoming medially
and posteriorly more flattened. Many of these animals are tubi-
colous. Some (e.g. Australonuphis) have a thin and ephemeral
tube. In others the tube is tough and may be highly charac-
teristic, such as in Hyalinoecia, which construct a cylindrical,
translucent, and quill-like tube (Pl. 6f), or in Nothria conchylega
where it is distinctly flattened with an inner lining of parchment
and large pieces of shells on the outside (PI. 6h). Live specimens
are iridescent and may have characteristic red or brown pigmen-
tation patterns, often as transverse segmental bands; others are
unpigmented (PI. 6f-h).

‘The prostomium is oval and anteriorly has a pair of round-
ed or elongated frontal lips, a pair of antero-lateral palps and
three more posterior antennae (Figs. 30.1a, 30.2a). The palps
and antennae are of similar shape with large and ringed cer-
atophores. What here are called frontal lips were in earlier
literature referred to as palps and what here are called palps
were referred to as antennae; Onuphidae were then considered
to have five antennae and a small pair of frontal palps or buc-
cal lips. Based on innervation studies, Orrhage (1995) argued
that the anterior lateral pair of these ‘antennae’ is homolo-
gous to the palps in other annelids and accordingly should be
referred to as such. The other structures were then referred to
as buccal lips by Orrhage (1995) and the upper pair renamed as
frontal lips by Paxton (1998). Eyes, when present, occur as a pair
of dorso-laterally situated spots, usually small. There appears
to be an often overlooked, second, smaller pair of eyes locat-
ed more anteriorly, in front of the antennae (von Palubitzki
and Purschke, 2020). Ultrastructure of the pigmented eyes in

Aponuphis bilineata is described in von Palubitzki and Purschke
(2020). The nuchal organs form ciliated bands along the dorso-
posterior side of the prostomium, mid-dorsally separated (Pax-
ton, 1986a; b). The peristomium forms a complete ring, with
(Figs. 30.1a, 30.2a) or without a pair of dorso-lateral elongat-
ed peristomial cirri (sometimes referred to as ‘tentacular cirri’).
Notopodia are represented only by dorsal cirri with or with-
out embedded aciculae (Figs. 30.1b, c). Emergent notochaetae
are absent. ‘The neuropodia have acicular, pre- and postchaetal
lobes, and ventral cirri. Branchiae occur in most Onuphidae as
simple or elaborate extensions of the dorsal cirri (Figs. 30.1b, c,
30.2b). Neurochaetae include multiple aciculae, dorsally situat-
ed limbate chaetae, pectinate chaetae, ventrally situated limbate
chaetae, and simple or ‘pseudocompound’ uni-, bi- or tridentate
hooks, which typically are hooded (Figs. 30.1d, 30.24). Anterior
segments deviate from following ones in many taxa, both in the
structure of parapodia and chaetae, and in being directed for
ward. The pygidium has one or two pairs of cirri; in the latter
case the dorsal pair is smaller.
The pharynx of Onuphidae is a ventral muscular pro-
boscis with an elaborate jaw apparatus (Haffner, 1959; Kielan-
Jaworowska, 1966; Paxton, 1986b). The mandibles (Fig. 30.1e)
consist of two elongated shafts, anteriorly ending in cutting
plates that are connected via a ligament (e.g, see Paxton, 1986b,
fig, 10). The maxillary apparatus (Fig. 30.11) is of the eulabidog-
nath type (Paxton, 2009) and consists of a pair of short carriers
and a variable number of maxillae which exhibit some differ-
ences between the left and right side. They are labelled from
posterior to anterior as MIL (maxillae I left) to MVL and MIR
to MVR (e.g, Paxton, 1986b, fig. 10b). The degree of scleroti-
zation of the jaws is highly variable; they are mineralized with
aragonite (Colbath, 1986). Morphogenesis of the jaws, their lar-
val shedding and ultrastructure is described in Vortsepneva et al.,
(2017) and in Paxton and Safarik (2008). The internal anatomy
of Onuphidae has been poorly studied. A gular membrane is
absent, and the gut is a straight tube (Fauchald and Rouse, 1997).
Corpora pedunculata are absent (Bullock and Horridge, 1965:
and references within). Details of the circulation system are
unknown, although dorsal and ventral blood vessels are present
(pers. obs.). Segmental filtration nephridia are metanephridia
(Goodrich, 1945).
